title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension presenting with isolated unilateral facial nerve palsy: a case report
case_prompt:
A 40-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of obesity (BMI 32) and hypertension presented with a 3-day history of a squeezing bifrontal headache that was gradual in onset and progressively worse. The headache was accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dizziness, transient visual disturbances in the right eye, and a feeling of bilateral ear fullness. One day before presentation, she noted numbness and weakness on the right side of her face, with difficulty closing the right eye and raising the right eyebrow. She denied diplopia, persistent vision loss, photophobia, tinnitus, fever, recent illness, tick bite, or other focal neurologic symptoms. She was not taking oral contraceptives.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Mental status and speech were normal, with no meningeal signs. Cranial nerve testing showed equal pupils reactive to light and accommodation, intact extraocular movements, and no abducens palsy. There was right-sided lower facial droop, decreased right eye closure, and impaired right forehead movement; facial sensation was intact bilaterally. Motor strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait were normal. Funduscopic examination revealed bilateral grade I–II papilledema.

A noncontrast head CT showed right pontomedullary hypodensity. Brain MRI with MR venography demonstrated stenosis of the lateral aspect of the transverse sinus, partial empty sella turcica, and mild papilledema, consistent with raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 28 cm H₂O; CSF cytology and chemistry were otherwise normal, with 2 white cells (100% lymphocytes), protein 24 mg/dL, 13 red cells, and glucose 58 mg/dL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Intracranial mass lesion or obstructive process was considered but ruled out by imaging — “imaging studies including CT scan and MRI/MRV ruled out structural and obstructive lesions and showed only signs of ICP, leaving the diagnosis of IIH as the most probable cause of this patient’s symptoms.”  
2. Brainstem stroke was entertained given pontomedullary hypodensity but excluded by the lack of supportive imaging or clinical stroke features — “consideration of other brain lesions legitimate, namely brainstem stroke and other structural lesions. These disorders were eventually ruled out by the absence of supporting features on the imaging studies and the clinical presentation as well.”  
3. Neurosarcoidosis was considered given cranial neuropathy but was unlikely without leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI and given its rarity — “MRI (with and without intravenously administered gadolinium) is the imaging modality of choice in the evaluation of NS, with the most common finding...linear enhancement along the brain contours….”  
4. Lyme disease was considered for isolated CN VII palsy but excluded by a normal CSF profile and absence of tick exposure or fever — “CNS Lyme disease is practically excluded in the presence of a completely normal CSF profile” and “the lack of a history of tick exposure or fever made Lyme disease even less likely in this patient.”  
5. Bell’s palsy coinciding with IIH was considered but deemed insufficient to explain headache or elevated ICP and supported by resolution with ICP reduction — “Bell’s palsy cannot explain this patient’s headache or the increase in ICP on its own.”  
6. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension was favored based on obesity, headache, transient visual disturbances, papilledema, and imaging signs of raised ICP — “IIH predominantly affects overweight and obese women of childbearing age” and “imaging studies…showed only signs of ICP, leaving the diagnosis of IIH as the most probable cause of this patient’s symptoms.”
